newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt's Mubarak anchors Middle East crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Egypt's Mubarak anchors Middle East crisis talks.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak anchored crisis talks in Cairo on Thursday with Arab leaders who said Israel was killing off the Middle East peace process.

Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri and Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara came to see Mubarak as a new row broke out in Israeli-Palestinian relations over an Israeli proposal to bypass interim withdrawals from the West Bank.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was expected in the afternoon and an Israeli spokeswoman said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would probably send his foreign policy adviser Dore Gold and possibly a foreign ministry official too.

Hariri, speaking after his meeting, reflected the Arab view that peace talks might not survive the crisis, which worsened this week when Israel began building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
"It's clear that Israel is taking hardline positions, and these positions, in the Egyptian leadership's opinion and ours, will help to bury the peace process and kill it off," he said.
"The Arabs are in accord in refusing to accept Israeli policy, in whole and in detail. Building settlements arouses Arab feelings and defies the world," he added.
Shara told reporters on arrival at Cairo airport that Egypt and Syria agreed the peace process was in crisis. Mubarak spoke to Syrian President Hafez al-Assad on Wednesday.

"The current situation...is a very explosive one due to the Israeli intransigence and expansionist policy. The Israeli prime minister bears responsibility for this and for all the dangers and setbacks that ensue," Shara added.
"The demarches that Egypt and Syria are making in Arab and world capitals are to alert international public opinion to the dangers of this period," he added.
Shara said consultations on a possible Arab summit "are underway". But Hariri said Mubarak did not discuss an Arab summit, which would be the first since one held in Cairo last June.
"It's clear that Arab leaders agree that Israeli behaviour is threatening the peace process. But it doesn't necessarily take an Arab summit to solve the problem," Hariri added.

Shara said Netanyahu had shown his attitude to peace this week by sending the bulldozers into the East Jerusalem area of Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa in Hebrew, where the Israelis intend to build 6,500 houses for Jews.

"(This) is in itself complete evidence that Netanyahu does not want peace. He is not working for peace. He is working for something else totally against the peace process. That is why we see that the peace process is in jeopardy," he said.
Egypt has also made dire predictions about the Middle East peace talks because of the settlement dispute.

Mubarak said on Wednesday Israel was leading the region back to violence. "If this settlement is built this will not be the end of the whole thing. It will be the beginning of a new era of violence which we would like to avoid," he said.
